candidate: Named job object per run via ctypes (Windows kernel32 API, Windows 8+ for nesting)
what: The supervisor creates a named job object, joins it before starting the training process, and any later controller call can open the job by name and terminate every member.
problem_here: Forced stop on native Windows uses taskkill with parent links and misses descendants whose parent exited; there are no POSIX process groups.
mechanism: CreateJobObjectW with a per-run name, AssignProcessToJobObject on the supervisor itself so children are members from birth, TerminateJobObject for forced stop; KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE (0x2000) left off by default so a run survives a supervisor crash.
evidence: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/procthread/job-objects and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/jobapi2/nf-jobapi2-createjobobjectw read 2026-11-11 (vendor documentation, no measurement); kit code read locally
maturity: Job objects exist since Windows 2000, nested jobs since Windows 8 (2012); operating-system API, no licence; adoption not measured today
cost: About 80 lines of ctypes with argtypes and error handling; failure modes: job creation refused, supervisor killed together with the run on forced stop, same-session requirement; no new attack surface beyond same-user process control
reason: Only standard-library way to stop a whole tree reliably without admin; taskkill stays as fallback.
cheap_local_trial: In a temporary project start a script that spawns a grandchild and then exits its middle process; force-stop by job name and check that no process is left.

candidate: Stop request file plus supervisor-delivered CTRL_BREAK inside a shared hidden console (CREATE_NO_WINDOW start)
what: Graceful stop on Windows: the controller writes a stop request file, the supervisor (which shares a windowless console with the run) sends CTRL_BREAK to the run's process group, then escalates after a deadline.
problem_here: Today expctl stop sends CTRL_BREAK from another console, which cannot arrive; the supervisor is detached, so the run gets its own visible console window.
mechanism: Start the supervisor with CREATE_NO_WINDOW (0x08000000) and CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP (0x200) instead of DETACHED_PROCESS; start the run with CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP only so it inherits the console; the supervisor already polls stop.json every 2 s and then calls os.kill(child_pid, signal.CTRL_BREAK_EVENT).
evidence: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/console/generateconsolectrlevent, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/console/creation-of-a-console and https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html (3.15.2) read 2026-11-11; vendor documentation, no measurement; failure of the current path inferred from kit code
maturity: Console control events and these flags predate Windows 10; Python exposes the flags since 3.7; operating-system API
cost: Small change to two Popen calls and the stop path; failure modes: handler delayed by native code, event also reaches worker processes in the group, up to 2 s polling delay; no new attack surface (a file in the run folder)
simpler_alternative: Forced kill only (loses the final checkpoint)
reason: The only documented way to deliver a graceful signal to a console program that has no visible shared console.
cheap_local_trial: Dummy run that handles SIGBREAK and writes a marker; request stop from a different terminal and from an agent tool call; check marker and exit record.

candidate: Cooperative stop: run-side logger polls the stop request file
what: The run-side logger checks for the stop request at each logging call and ends the loop at a step boundary, before any signal is sent.
problem_here: A group-wide console event also reaches data-loader workers, which exit at once; signals do not exist in one form across schedulers, containers and remote machines.
mechanism: One stat call per logging step on a file in the run folder; the signal becomes the second stage and the forced kill the third.
evidence: Inferred from https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/console/generateconsolectrlevent (group delivery) and https://docs.python.org/3/library/signal.html (handlers wait for native code), read 2026-11-11; nobody measured the worker-exit effect
maturity: n/a (practice); a stop-file check is a long-standing pattern
cost: A few lines in runlog.py; one stat call per logging step; failure mode: scripts that log rarely react late, hence the signal stage
reason: Same graceful path on every platform and backend; removes the worker fan-out risk if the trial confirms it.
cheap_local_trial: Two-worker data loader on Windows: compare stop by file with stop by CTRL_BREAK and look for worker errors before the checkpoint.

candidate: Process identity as PID plus kernel start time from the standard library on each OS
what: Record and compare the process creation time without psutil: GetProcessTimes on Windows, /proc/<pid>/stat field 22 on Linux, ps -o lstart= on macOS.
problem_here: Without psutil the kit has no start time on Windows and macOS, so a recycled PID is accepted as the run and could be signalled or reported alive.
mechanism: OpenProcess with PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION (0x1000), GetProcessTimes creation FILETIME; exact comparison of the raw value on the same machine; WaitForSingleObject for liveness instead of the exit-code-259 test.
evidence: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-getprocesstimes read 2026-11-11 (vendor documentation); Linux and macOS parts from memory, not re-read today; gap confirmed in kit code
maturity: Operating-system APIs present in all supported Windows versions; the /proc format has been stable for decades
cost: About 40 lines of ctypes plus a ps call on macOS; failure modes: access denied on foreign processes, locale-dependent ps output, launcher shim PID differs from interpreter PID
reason: Closes PID reuse on every platform with one tested code path.
cheap_local_trial: Edit the stored start value in pid.json of a live dummy run and confirm the controller reports not-the-same-process on Windows and WSL.

candidate: Bounded retry around os.replace and tolerant state readers
what: Writers retry the atomic replace on permission errors with short backoff; readers open, read, close and retry.
problem_here: write_json_atomic calls os.replace once; on Windows a concurrent reader or a scanner holding the target makes it fail and a status or exit record is lost.
mechanism: Temporary file in the same folder, fsync, os.replace in a loop on PermissionError for a few seconds; never delete-then-rename.
evidence: https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html (3.15.2) for atomic replace; https://github.com/isaacs/node-graceful-fs/blob/main/polyfills.js (commit f7a4370) retries rename for up to 60 s citing antivirus locks; read 2026-11-11; the sharing-violation behaviour itself was not re-read in a primary source
maturity: n/a (practice); the retry precedent sits in a library used across the Node.js ecosystem
cost: About 15 lines; failure mode: a long-held lock still fails after the deadline and must be reported, not swallowed
reason: Cheap, and removes a class of intermittent Windows failures that would corrupt run accounting.
cheap_local_trial: One process rewrites a state file 1000 times while another reads it in a loop on Windows; count failures with and without the retry.

candidate: Link-free snapshot: copy tracked files, junction for linked directories, hard link or copy for linked files
what: Replace symbolic links in the run snapshot on Windows with junctions (directories) and hard links (files on the same volume), falling back to copy or a clear error.
problem_here: launch exits 6 on native Windows because the account cannot create symbolic links; only 18 of 139 baseline checks pass there.
mechanism: mklink /J through cmd for directories, os.link for files, shutil.copy2 fallback under a size cap; cleanup tests the reparse attribute and never descends into links; linked paths are recorded in the run metadata.
evidence: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/hard-links-and-junctions and https://docs.python.org/3/library/shutil.html (3.15.2, junction-safe rmtree since 3.8) read 2026-11-11; baseline failure measured by the kit owner on 2026-11-10 (docs/upgrade/BASELINE.md)
maturity: NTFS junctions and hard links exist since Windows 2000; Python os.link on Windows since 3.2
cost: Moderate: new snapshot branch plus safe cleanup and traversal; failure modes: cross-volume or network targets, live view lets a run change the original, volumes without link support; attack surface: a junction pointing outside the tree if paths are not validated
simpler_alternative: Plain copies of everything (slow and large for data folders)
reason: Makes native Windows launch work without admin while keeping snapshots cheap; needs the junction trial first.
cheap_local_trial: In a temporary folder create a junction and a hard link as the ordinary test account, on the system volume and on a second volume, then remove the snapshot and confirm the originals are intact.

candidate: git worktree as snapshot mechanism (git 2.56.0 documentation)
what: Create each run's code snapshot as a linked worktree at a commit.
problem_here: Candidate replacement for the symbolic-link snapshot on Windows.
mechanism: git worktree add --detach creates a checkout that shares the object store.
evidence: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree (2.56.0) read 2026-11-11: only clean worktrees can be removed, submodule support is incomplete; the page says nothing about ignored files (inferred: not carried over)
maturity: Part of git since 2.5 (2015); GPL-2.0; widely used
cost: Requires a commit for every run, writes metadata into the user's repository, leaves entries to prune after crashes; does not bring data or other ignored paths
simpler_alternative: Copy tracked files as the kit already does
reason: Adds repository side effects and still needs links or copies for ignored inputs.
cheap_local_trial: None needed; revisit only if copying tracked files proves too slow on large repositories.

candidate: Copy-on-write copies (Windows block cloning on ReFS or Dev Drive, Linux reflink)

cheap_local_trial: Time shutil.copy2 of a 5 GB file on an ordinary NTFS volume and, if one exists, on a Dev Drive.

candidate: Claude Code exec-form hooks (command plus args, no shell)

evidence: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks (mentions versions up to 2.1.314) read 2026-11-11; vendor documentation; the version that introduced args and its support in agent front matter were not found

reason: Removes shell parsing and quoting differences across platforms.

candidate: Codex hook entries with commandWindows override
what: Give each Codex hook a POSIX command and a separate Windows command.
problem_here: Codex runs hook commands through cmd on Windows, where POSIX syntax and python3 fail, and a failing pre-tool hook lets the tool run.

cheap_local_trial: Temporary project on Windows: interpreter path with and without spaces, confirm the hook runs and blocks.

candidate: Cursor hook entries that PowerShell accepts, with failClosed
what: Write Cursor hook commands in a form valid under PowerShell and mark the guard hook fail-closed.
problem_here: Cursor on Windows runs hooks through PowerShell and ignores hook failures by default, so a broken interpreter silently removes the guard.

maturity: Documented feature; first version not checked
cost: PowerShell and POSIX forms differ, so the installer writes per-machine entries; fail-closed can lock the user out
simpler_alternative: Same command as for the other agents
reason: Needed for an enforced guard on the editor agent on Windows.
cheap_local_trial: Temporary project on Windows: point the hook at a missing interpreter and confirm the action is denied.
